title: Welcome to Setpoint Labs.
This is the Foundation level, and it is where your journey into industrial automation begins.
In the next few minutes, I will show you what you are going to learn, how the lectures work, and what you will be able to do by the end.
why: Every mine, factory, bottling plant and water works in South Africa runs on controllers.
Conveyors start and stop, pumps fill tanks, and motors spin, because a small computer is watching the sensors and making decisions.
That computer is called a programmable logic controller, or P L C.
And the people who can program and fault find them are scarce, and in demand.
scan: A P L C works in a simple loop called the scan.
First, it reads every input, like push buttons and sensors.
Then it runs your program, from top to bottom.
Finally, it writes the outputs, switching contactors, valves and lights.
Then it does it all again, many times every second.
Once you understand the scan, everything else in this course makes sense.
ladder: You will program the P L C in ladder logic, the language electricians already think in.
Here is the most famous circuit in the trade.
Press Start, and power flows through the Stop contact to the motor coil.
The motor's own contact then holds the circuit in, so the motor keeps running when you let go.
Press Stop, and the circuit breaks.
This is called a seal in, and you will build it yourself in module four.
stage1a: The Foundation level has two stages. Stage one is Fundamentals and Skayda, with ten modules.
Module one, what a P L C is. Why machines need controllers, what is inside the P L C, and how inputs, outputs and the scan fit together.
Module two, ladder logic basics. Ladder symbols, contacts and coils, and latch and unlatch.
Module three, numbers, data and tags. Bits, bytes and words, data types, and tags, addresses and memory.
Module four, motor control. The seal in circuit, overload protection, and jog and run.
Module five, field devices. Buttons, selector switches and limit switches, proximity and photoelectric sensors, and relays, contactors and solenoid valves.
stage1b: Module six, timers. On delay and off delay timers, and pilot lamps and alarms.
Module seven, counters, edges and comparisons. Counting parts, detecting edges, and comparisons and maths.
Module eight, safety basics. Emergency stop circuits, and safe stop design.
Module nine, pneumatics. Compressed air and cylinders, and solenoid valves with cylinder sequences.
And module ten, your first look at H M I and Skayda. What they are, your first operator screen, and alarms and trends.
stage2: Stage two is Installation and Commissioning. This is where theory meets the panel.
Module one, drawings. Reading a schematic, power and control circuits, and panel layout with terminal numbering.
Module two, electrical safety at work. Isolation, lockout and testing for dead, protection devices and earthing, and cables, glands and wiring standards.
Module three, wiring and testing. Wiring P L C inputs and outputs, testing with a multimeter, and I O loop checks.
And module four, software and commissioning. Projects, download and online monitoring, a commissioning checklist, a fault finding method, and backups and change control.
format: Every lecture follows the same steady pattern.
We start with why it matters, then the theory, with drawings.
Next, we meet the parts on a 3D machine, build the logic step by step, and run it.
We then break things on purpose, so you learn to find faults.
Finally, we show the same logic on Siemens S7 twelve hundred and Allen Bradley CompactLogix, and you finish with a lab and a short quiz.
outcome: By the end of the Foundation level, you will understand how a P L C controls a machine, read and write ladder logic, read drawings, wire and test I O, and commission a simple machine safely.
The Foundation exam has a sixty minute theory paper, and a ninety minute practical task on a simulated motor starter and conveyor.
You need seventy percent on each part to earn your certificate.
close: Everything here is simulated training. It builds real skill, but it is not permission to work on live plant.
Always follow your site's rules, and work under supervision.
Right, let us begin. Our first lecture is, why machines need controllers.
